ARTICLE IN PRESS The Impact of Social Support on Quality of Life in Chinese Parents of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: The Mediating Role of Resilience Abstract This study examined how resilience mediates the relationship between social support and quality of life (QoL) among parents of children with autism spectrum disorder (CWASD) in China. A total of 257 parents were recruited using simple random sampling from a hospital. Participants completed the Social Support Rating Scale (SSRS), the Connor-Davidson S Resilience Scale (CD-RISC, Chinese version), and the World Health Organization Quality of S E Life-BREF (WHOQOL-BREF, Chinese Version). Data were analyzed using SPSS 22.0, R P including descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and mediating effect analysis with the N PROCESS macro. Social support was positIively correlated with resilience (r = 0.60, p < 0.01) E and all QoL domains, with correlation coefficients ranging from 0.48 to 0.67 (all p < 0.05). L C Mediating effect analysis reveaIled that resilience partially mediated the effect of social support T R on QoL (β = 0.61, t = 4.55, p < 0.001; indirect effect = 0.21, 95% CI [0.06, 0.13]). This study A reveals that resilience is a crucial pathway through which social support is translated into improved QoL for parents of CWASD. This finding underscores the need for a dual-focus approach in interventions, one that simultaneously strengthens external support systems and cultivates internal coping capacities. Introduction 1.1 Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that begins in the early developmental period and is defined by a dual impairment: persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, alongside a pattern of restricted behaviors, fixated interests, inflexible routines, and atypical sensory responses (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). Globally, the World Health Organization (WHO, 2023) estimates that approximately 1 in 100 S children is diagnosed with ASD. A clear upward trend in prevalence has been observed in many S E regions. For instance, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (2024) reports a R P significantly higher rate of 1 in 36 eight-year-old children in the United States. Similar N increases are noted in other high-income reIgions, such as Europe and Australia (Zeidan et al., E 2022). In China, the scale is also substantial: the China Disabled Persons’ Federation (2024) L C reports over 13 million diagnoIsed individuals, of whom approximately 3 million are children, T R with an estimated 200,000 new cases annually. At present, there is no known cure for ASD. A Mainstream approaches rely on long-term institutional and family-based interventions aimed at improving functional abilities (Gao et al., 2023). Despite increasing global awareness, significant cross-national disparities remain in diagnostic access, availability of early intervention services, and the strength of caregiver support systems. These challenges are particularly acute in low- and middle-income countries, including China, where systemic limitations in healthcare and social welfare infrastructures may hinder timely diagnosis and comprehensive family support (Gao et al., 2023). 1.2 Parents of Children with ASD (CWASD) ARTICLE IN PRESS The diagnosis of a child with ASD introduces profound and unique challenges for parents, which are intrinsically linked to the core characteristics of ASD (Shorey et al., 2020). For instance, the high prevalence of challenging behaviors in CWASD, such as aggression, self- injury, dietary problems, and sleep problems, requires constant vigilance and crisis management from parents, leading to physical and emotional exhaustion (S. Bonis, 2016; S. A. Bonis & Sawin, 2016; Han & Gao, 2025; Martin et al., 2019). This relentless caregiving demand, compounded by the chronic nature of the condition and the absence of a cure, S contributes directly to the elevated rates of anxiety, depression, and chronic stress observed in S E this population (Falk et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2023). Furthermore, parents may withdraw from R P social participation due to difficulties in managing their child’s behavior in public, fear of social N stigma, or the inherent challenges in findingI inclusive activities, resulting in shrinking informal E support networks (Gao & Drani, 2025; Shorey et al., 2020). These multifaceted pressures L C frequently disrupt marital andI family relationships (Robinson & Neece, 2015; Shorey et al., T R 2020). Recent studies have increasingly focused on resilience as a protective factor that A moderates these effects (Cheatham & Fernando, 2022; Hassanein et al., 2021; Sardohan Yildirim et al., 2025). However, despite these advances, there remains a limited understanding of how external resources (e.g., social support) and internal capacities (e.g., resilience) interact to shape the quality of life (QoL) of these parents. Given that the stressors they encounter are directly rooted in the complex, multidimensional features of ASD, elucidating these relationships is critical for developing effective support strategies. 1.3 Social Support and QoL in Parents of CWASD Social support is widely conceptualized as a multidimensional construct comprising ARTICLE IN PRESS emotional, informational, appraisal, and instrumental components. It serves as a critical external resource that enables individuals and families to navigate psychological stress and social adversity (T. S. M. Wong & Shorey, 2022). Empirical research has demonstrated that social support is a key determinant of parental adaptation and overall well-being. Among parents of CWASD and other developmental disabilities, higher levels of perceived or received support are associated with reduced parenting stress, lower levels of psychological distress, and enhanced QoL (Gallagher & Whiteley, 2013; Kuru & Piyal, 2018; Yorke et al., 2018). S These effects are facilitated through both formal mechanisms (e.g., public services, peer S E networks) and informal ties (e.g., extended family, community relations). In this literature, QoL R P is commonly conceptualized as a multidimensional outcome encompassing physical, N psychological, social, and environmental doImains. It is typically assessed using standardized E instruments such as the World Health Organization Quality of Life-BREF (WHOQOL-BREF), L C which provides an integrative Iframework for evaluating the broader impacts of caregiving on T R daily life (Kuhlthau et al., 2014; WHO, 2012). A However, the structure and accessibility of social support in China differ markedly from those in high-income countries, shaped by both institutional limitations and culturally embedded caregiving norms (Sun et al., 2019). While public awareness of ASD has improved, many parents, particularly those in rural or under-resourced regions, continue to face substantial barriers in accessing timely diagnoses, affordable intervention services, and sustained professional assistance (Feng, Chen, et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2023). Culturally, prevailing values that emphasize family self-reliance, emotional suppression, and the concealment of disability-related challenges often inhibit help-seeking behaviors (Ng & Ng, ARTICLE IN PRESS 2022; Tait et al., 2014, 2016). As a result, social support for parents of CWASD in China remains predominantly family-based, with limited engagement in formal support systems or structured peer networks. This absence of diversified support pathways not only intensifies caregiving burdens but also restricts access to coping resources that are essential for maintaining well-being. These structural and cultural barriers have direct implications for parental QoL. Studies using the WHOQOL-BREF have consistently shown that Chinese parents of CWASD report significantly lower scores in the psychological, social relationship, S and environmental domains compared to population norms (Guan et al., 2015). Parents S E consistently experience persistent emotional strain, diminished social connectedness, and R P reduced access to health care, education, and financial assistance. In this context, QoL reflects N not only individual-level psychological outIcomes but also broader sociocultural and systemic E inequities that shape how caregiving is experienced and managed. L C 1.4 Social Support, QoL, andI Resilience in Parents of CWASD T R Resilience is commonly defined as an individual’s capacity to maintain or regain A psychological well-being in the face of adversity by mobilizing internal strengths and adaptive coping strategies (Walsh, 2021). This capacity is shaped by person–environment interactions and varies across individuals depending on contextual factors such as life experiences, available resources, and social roles (Walsh, 2021). In caregiving contexts, resilience has been associated with more effective emotional regulation, reduced psychological distress, and better QoL outcomes (Cheatham & Fernando, 2022). Among parents of CWASD, resilience plays a particularly vital role in managing the long- term and often unpredictable demands of caregiving. Studies have shown that these parents ARTICLE IN PRESS tend to exhibit lower levels of resilience compared to parents of typically developing children, as they face persistent challenges related to emotional strain, social stigma, and uncertain developmental trajectories (Chen et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2023). Nevertheless, resilience can be fostered through adaptive family processes, such as shifts in belief systems, improved communication patterns, and flexible caregiving arrangements, which in turn enhance parental ability to sustain caregiving and engage constructively with external resources (Sardohan Yildirim et al., 2025; Walsh, 2021). S Social support and resilience do not operate in isolation. Evidence indicates that higher S E levels of perceived or received social support are positively associated with both physical and R P mental health among parents of CWASD (Hassanein et al., 2021; Kuru & Piyal, 2018; Wang N et al., 2022). In contrast, insufficient suIpport can further undermine resilience, thereby E intensifying the psychological burden of caregiving. Recent studies suggest that enhancing L C both external support systems Iand internal coping resources is essential for improving parental T R QoL (Fallahchai & Fallahi, 2022; Yang et al., 2018). Rather than functioning as separate A domains, social support and resilience may be best understood as interdependent components that collectively shape the caregiving experience. From a process-oriented perspective, resilience may serve as a mediating mechanism that explains how social support is translated into psychological adaptation and well-being (Cheatham & Fernando, 2022; Hassanein et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2018). Accordingly, the present study adopts an integrated approach to examine how social support and resilience jointly influence the QoL of parents of CWASD, with a particular focus on their interactive and mediating effects. This provides a foundation for the development of a ARTICLE IN PRESS contextually informed theoretical framework and a testable model of parental well-being. 1.5 Theoretical Framework and Research Questions To enhance the conceptual coherence of the present study, Bronfenbrenner’s (2000) ecological systems theory is adopted as the guiding theoretical framework. This theory conceptualizes individual development and well-being as embedded within a nested structure of environmental systems, ranging from the immediate microsystem (e.g., parent–child interactions, spousal relationships) to the broader macrosystem (e.g., cultural beliefs, social S norms, disability-related policies). Within this framework, social support is understood as a S E multilevel construct encompassing both microsystemic sources (e.g., support from family and R P close peers) and exosystemic provisions (e.g., institutional services and policy infrastructure). N Meanwhile, resilience is viewed as an adapItive capacity developed through dynamic person– E environment interactions across these systems. QoL, the core outcome variable, is shaped by L C the interplay of these contextuaIl (external) and psychological (internal) factors. This ecological T R lens provides a multilayered perspective for understanding how external social resources and A internal psychological strengths jointly influence caregiving outcomes in parents of CWASD. This theoretical positioning aligns with Cheatham and Fernando (2022), Hassanein et al. (2021), and Yang et al. (2018), who conceptualize resilience not as a fixed trait, but as a dynamic mediator that shapes developmental and adaptive outcomes across ecological systems. Given the theoretical positioning of resilience as a dynamic internal capacity influenced by external social systems, a mediation model is theoretically well-suited to examine the pathways through which social support affects parental QoL. Guided by this theoretical orientation, the present study focuses on the population of ARTICLE IN PRESS parents of CWASD in China. It examines the current status and interrelations among their social support, resilience, and QoL, and further investigates the mediating role of resilience in the relationship between social support and QoL. The conceptual model is illustrated in Figure 1. The findings are expected to not only contribute novel insights to the international literature on family stress and coping but also to inform the development of culturally sensitive, evidence- based interventions for families of CWASD across diverse socioeconomic and cultural settings. Method A 2.1 Sampling Procedure This study employed a simple random sampling technique to recruit participants from the Fifth Hospital of Yulin City, a legally certified institution in Yulin City, China, specializing in the diagnosis and rehabilitation of individuals with ASD. The hospital provided the full sampling frame, comprising families registered for ASD-related services whose children had been formally diagnosed and were receiving ongoing rehabilitation. Inclusion criteria for participant selection were as follows: i) Parents of children aged 0– 18 years, in accordance with the Law of the People’s Republic of China on the Protection of ARTICLE IN PRESS Minors and the Law on Compulsory Education (Central People’s Government of the People’s Republic of China, 2020, 2021), with a formal diagnosis of ASD issued by a statutory medical institution. ii) Parents with a minimum education level of primary school, to ensure their ability to understand the questionnaire and provide independent responses without assistance. iii) Only biological parents or legal guardians were included, as they are legally recognized as the primary caregivers and decision-makers in matters concerning the child’s health, education, and daily care responsibilities. S Exclusion criteria were as follows: i) Parents who themselves had a diagnosed severe S E psychiatric disorder (e.g., schizophrenia, bipolar disorder) that could significantly confound R P the assessment of their QoL, resilience, and social support. ii) Parents of children diagnosed N with severe, co-occurring physical, geneticI, or neurological conditions (e.g., cerebral palsy, E Down syndrome) that would introduce caregiving demands substantially different from those L C primarily associated with ASDI. T R 2.2 Data Collection A Data were collected between late November and early December 2024 in the outpatient rehabilitation department of the hospital. A total of 270 paper-based questionnaires were randomly distributed from the list of eligible families. Surveys were administered on-site in private consultation rooms to ensure confidentiality and minimize distractions. Trained research assistants (postgraduate students majoring in social work and psychology) were responsible for administering the questionnaires, briefing participants on the purpose of the study, and providing clarification for any survey items when necessary. Each parent completed the questionnaire independently in a private setting and returned it on-site. ARTICLE IN PRESS All 270 questionnaires were retrieved. After excluding responses with missing data or procedural inconsistencies, a total of 257 valid questionnaires were retained, yielding an effective response rate of 95.19%. Although no a priori power analysis was conducted, a post hoc calculation using G*Power 3.1 indicated that this sample size exceeds the minimum requirement for detecting medium effect sizes (f² = 0.15) at 95% power and α = 0.05 in multiple regression models with three predictors. This suggests that the study had sufficient statistical power to test the proposed model and hypotheses. Y. Wong et al., 2018). This study employed the T R Chinese version of the WHOQOL-BREF, which consists of 26 items measuring four domains: A physical health, psychological well-being, social relationships, and environmental conditions, along with two general items assessing overall quality of life and perceived health status (WHO, 2012). Each item is rated on a 5-point Likert scale, and higher scores indicate better perceived quality of life. The psychometric properties of the Chinese version have been well validated. A validation study conducted by Leung et al. (2005) in Hong Kong using the Chinese version demonstrated good construct validity. Cronbach’s alpha for the four domains ranged from 0.73 to 0.83, and the test–retest reliability was 0.83. A national survey by Guan et al. (2015) reported Cronbach’s alpha of 0.81 for the overall scale, with subscale Cronbach’s alpha ranging from ARTICLE IN PRESS 0.73 to 0.79, further supporting the applicability of the instrument among Chinese populations. Permission to use this instrument was formally obtained from the WHO (Request ID: 202403574). In the current sample, the Cronbach’s alpha for the overall WHOQOL-BREF was 0.89, and the alphas for the four domains (physical, psychological, social, and environmental) were 0.82, 0.85, 0.79, and 0.80, respectively, demonstrating good internal consistency in our sample. 2.3.2 The Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (CD-RISC, Chinese Version) S The CD-RISC is a widely used instrument for measuring individual resilience and S E psychological adaptability (Connor & Davidson, 2003). This study adopted the 25-item R P Chinese version revised by Yu and Zhang (2007), rated on a 5-point Likert scale, with higher N scores reflecting greater individual resilienIce. The Chinese version demonstrated excellent E internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.91). The validity of Chinese version was also L C satisfying in terms of the actuIal data matching the expected correlation between resilience T R measure and the variables of self-esteem, life satisfaction, and personality trait factors of NEO A Five-Factor Inventory (Yu & Zhang, 2007). In the current sample, the Cronbach’s alpha for the CD-RISC was 0.88, indicating high reliability. 2.3.3 Social Support Rating Scale (SSRS) This study employed the SSRS, a 10-item instrument developed by Xiao (1994) to assess perceived social support within the Chinese sociocultural context. The SSRS comprises three subscales: objective support, subjective support, and utilization of support. Higher scores on both the total scale and its subdomains indicate greater levels of social support. The SSRS has demonstrated satisfactory psychometric properties. Xiao (1994) reported an internal ARTICLE IN PRESS consistency coefficient (Cronbach’s alpha) of 0.89 and test–retest reliability of 0.92. In the current sample, the Cronbach’s alpha for the total SSRS was 0.90. The subscales of objective support, subjective support, and utilization of support yielded alphas of 0.82, 0.87, and 0.78, respectively, confirming the instrument’s reliability. 2.4 Data Analysis Data analysis was conducted using SPSS 22.0. The analytical procedure followed several sequential steps. First, preliminary analyses were conducted to ensure the data met the S assumptions for parametric testing. Normality was assessed by examining skewness and S E kurtosis statistics for all primary variables. Following established guidelines (Kline, 2023), R P absolute values for skewness less than 2 and for kurtosis less than 4 were considered indicative N of a normal distribution. Residual plotIs were also checked to assess linearity and E homoscedasticity for regression analyses. All assumptions were adequately met. Second, L C descriptive statistics (means aInd standard deviations) were computed for the primary study T R variables. Third, Pearson’s correlation coefficients were calculated to assess the bivariate A associations among the total scores of social support, resilience, and each domain of QoL. Finally, mediating effects analysis was conducted using Model 4 of the PROCESS macro for SPSS (Hayes, 2022). Social support (SSRS total score) was entered as the independent variable, QoL (computed as the sum of four WHOQOL-BREF domain scores) as the dependent variable, and resilience (CD-RISC total score) as the mediator. Standardized coefficients were reported, and the statistical significance of the indirect effect was tested using bootstrap resampling (5,000 samples) with 95% confidence intervals. 3. Discussions R A This study explored the relationship between social support, QoL, and resilience among parents of CWASD in China and found the following main outcomes: 4.1 Social Support Affects QoL Through a Partially Mediating Effect of Resilience The findings indicate that resilience partially mediates the relationship between social support and QoL among parents of CWASD. This suggests that social support functions not only as a direct protective factor but also as a foundation for developing internal coping resources. According to Bronfenbrenner’s (2000) ecological systems theory, resilience emerges from ongoing interactions between individuals and their immediate and extended social environments. When parents of CWASD receive sufficient emotional, informational, appraisal, ARTICLE IN PRESS and instrumental support, they are more likely to reinterpret caregiving stress, maintain psychological stability, and adopt adaptive strategies that enhance their well-being. This is consistent with Walsh’s (2021) conceptualization of resilience as a dynamic process shaped by relational and contextual factors. In the Chinese context, this process may be shaped by sociocultural norms that emphasize emotional control, family-centered caregiving, and reluctance to seek external help. As a result, social support is often underutilized or internalized indirectly, contributing to greater S psychological burden (Ng & Ng, 2022; Tait et al., 2016). Resilience, in this case, becomes a S E key mediator that enables parents of CWASD to maintain caregiving roles while navigating R P limited external resources. This finding helps explain why interventions that solely provide N informational or material support may be inIsufficient unless they also enhance psychological E adaptability and self-efficacy (Sardohan Yildirim et al., 2025). L C Furthermore, differences Ibetween the present findings and some prior studies may reflect T R variations in how resilience is operationalized across contexts. In this study, the CD-RISC was A used, which emphasizes personal strength, tenacity, and optimism. Other studies may adopt family-based or community-based definitions of resilience, leading to divergent results (Cheatham & Fernando, 2022). Additionally, access to ASD intervention services and parent training programs varies widely across countries and regions, potentially influencing how social support is experienced and translated into resilience. Together, these findings highlight the need for culturally responsive, multidimensional support strategies. Improving QoL for CWASD parents requires not only increasing support access but also fostering resilience through psychological, relational, and contextual pathways. ARTICLE IN PRESS 4.2 Multidimensional Effects of Social Support and Resilience on QoL Subdomain analyses revealed that social support significantly predicted multiple domains of QoL, including physical, psychological, social relationships, and environmental aspects. This finding aligns with Margalit’s (2010) theory of the multidimensional function of social support in promoting mental health and psychosocial adjustment. Notably, psychological and social relationship domains showed the strongest associations, suggesting that interpersonal connectedness and emotional coping resources may play a more immediate role in buffering S parental stress than structural or material conditions. S E Resilience was also a significant predictor of psychological well-being and social R P relationships, indicating that internal psychological adaptability contributes more directly to N emotional and relational stability than to pIhysical or environmental conditions. This pattern E may reflect the Chinese caregiving context, where emotional regulation and interpersonal L C harmony are culturally emphasIized (Ng & Ng, 2022), while external systems such as education, T R healthcare, and disability services remain unevenly accessible (Feng, Chen, et al., 2022). These A findings may also be influenced by the methodological focus of the instruments used; for instance, the CD-RISC centers on individual-level psychological traits, which may limit its explanatory power for environmental QoL. Future studies should consider integrating structural-level indicators and culturally adapted resilience constructs to fully capture the ecological complexity of caregiving QoL. 4.3 Cultural and Structural Constraints on Social Support This study highlights how cultural values and policy-level structures jointly constrain the social support available to parents of CWASD in China. Culturally, traditional beliefs shaped ARTICLE IN PRESS by Confucian values emphasize family responsibility, emotional restraint, and parental sacrifice, often framing caregiving as a private moral obligation rather than a shared social responsibility (Tait et al., 2014). These expectations discourage help-seeking behaviors, particularly among mothers, who are commonly regarded as the primary caregivers. Fear of stigma and “loss of face” associated with disability further limits parents’ willingness to disclose their child’s diagnosis or access formal services (Ng & Ng, 2022). This can result in concealment of the child’s condition, missed intervention opportunities, and diminished S informal support from extended kin or communities (Gao et al., 2023; Tait et al., 2016). S E At the structural level, despite recent improvements in ASD awareness and service R P provision, access to educational, medical, and rehabilitative resources remains uneven, N especially in under-resourced regions (FengI, Zhou, et al., 2022). Although national and local E policies provide certain supports, such as subsidies or funding for institutional care, the L C implementation is often fragmeInted across regions, leading to inconsistent service delivery and T R limited reach (Liu & Fisher, 2023). Moreover, existing policy frameworks primarily focus on A children’s diagnosis and treatment, offering minimal psychological or social support to caregivers themselves (Wu et al., 2010). These limitations underscore a critical gap between the multifaceted needs of families and the narrow scope of current support systems. Taken together, these findings suggest that interventions aiming to improve parental QoL must address both cultural stigma and structural fragmentation. Beyond individual-level training, efforts should include community awareness campaigns, stigma reduction programs, and more inclusive, caregiver-oriented policy reforms that expand service equity across diverse regions and populations. ARTICLE IN PRESS 4.4 Practical Significance The findings of this study, particularly the mediating role of resilience, offer several concrete implications for the design of evidence-informed interventions for parents of CWASD. First, to directly enhance social support, service providers should move beyond general resource provision to establish structured support systems. Peer-led support groups, for example, can create safe spaces where parents share experiences, reduce stigma, and build a sense of community. Given the geographical and social barriers many families face, developing S moderated digital platforms and online communities is also a critical strategy. These platforms S E can offer accessible, 24/7 peer support, expert-led webinars, and a repository of verified R P informational resources, thereby addressing both subjective and objective support needs. N Second, the finding that resilience is a kIey mediator underscores the need for interventions E that explicitly target and cultivate this internal capacity. This goes beyond simple L C psychoeducation. Structured rIesilience training programs, grounded in cognitive-behavioral T R principles, should be developed. Such programs could focus on teaching parents practical skills A in emotional regulation, cognitive reframing of stressors, problem-solving, and mindfulness. By strengthening these core psychological skills, parents are better equipped to translate available social support into improved well-being. Third, our mediation model suggests that the most effective approach is an integrated one. Rather than offering disconnected services, a holistic intervention model is recommended. For instance, community-based family centers could serve as hubs that offer both peer-led support groups and professional-led resilience training workshops. This integrated model ensures that as parents receive external support, they are simultaneously empowered with the internal skills ARTICLE IN PRESS needed to effectively utilize that support, maximizing the positive impact on their QoL. Finally, to accelerate the development of such interventions, it is beneficial to adapt established, evidence-based models from other countries. For instance, the Stepping Stones Triple P (SSTP) program, an internationally recognized parent training intervention, equips parents with positive parenting strategies to manage challenging behaviors, thereby reducing parental stress and enhancing family functioning (Tellegen & Sanders, 2013). Similarly, Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) programs have demonstrated effectiveness in S improving the psychological well-being and resilience of parents of CWASD by teaching S E mindfulness skills to cope with chronic stress (Rojas-Torres et al., 2021). The adaptation of R P these models for Chinese caregivers would require careful cultural tailoring. For example, N parenting strategies in SSTP could be modIified to align with Chinese cultural values, while E MBSR could be framed to resonate with traditional contemplative practices. Furthermore, L C delivering these programs throIugh digital platforms could help overcome barriers of stigma T R and geographical distance, making support more accessible to a wider range of families in A China. 4.5 Limitations and Directions for Future Research This study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, the sample was drawn from a single region in China, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to the broader population of parents of CWASD. Future research should consider recruiting participants from multiple geographic and cultural regions to capture a more diverse range of experiences and improve external validity. Second, the study’s cross-sectional design represents a primary limitation, as it precludes the establishment of causal relationships. This ARTICLE IN PRESS is particularly relevant because the associations among social support, resilience, and QoL are likely reciprocal. For instance, while our model posits that social support enhances QoL, it is equally plausible that parents with a higher QoL are better equipped to build and maintain social networks. The unidirectional pathway tested in this study was nonetheless specified based on a robust theoretical foundation; foundational frameworks, such as ecological systems theory and stress-buffering models, provide a logical and parsimonious starting point. Nevertheless, future longitudinal research is essential to disentangle the temporal ordering and S formally test for the bidirectional dynamics of these relationships over time. Third, the study S E focused exclusively on social support and resilience as explanatory variables. While these are R P important factors, the quality of life of parents of CWASD is likely influenced by a broader N constellation of variables, including family fIunctioning, cultural values, caregiving burden, and E access to institutional or policy support. Future research should incorporate these additional L C dimensions to provide a moreI comprehensive explanatory framework. Finally, this study did T R not include a contemporaneous control group of parents of typically developing children. This A cross-sectional, single-group design limits the ability to definitively attribute the observed levels of QoL, resilience, and social support specifically to the experience of parenting a child with ASD, as opposed to general parenting stressors. Future studies are encouraged to employ a case-control design with a carefully matched reference group to better isolate the unique challenges associated with ASD caregiving. 5. Conclusions This study reveals a key mechanism underlying the well-being of parents of CWASD, demonstrating that resilience is a crucial pathway through which social support is translated ARTICLE IN PRESS into improved QoL. The findings clarify that social support does not operate in isolation; its benefits are significantly amplified when parents possess the internal capacity to effectively utilize these external resources. This underscores the necessity of a dual-focus approach in intervention design: simultaneously bolstering external support systems while actively cultivating parents’ internal resilience. By providing robust empirical evidence for this mediation model within a non-Western context, this research not only offers a valuable foundation for developing targeted, evidence-based practices in China but also enriches the S international literature on family stress and coping mechanisms. JSON: Name: social_support_resilience_qol_mediation Title: Cross-sectional mediation analysis of resilience in the effect of social support on quality of life among Chinese parents of children with autism spectrum disorder Short Hypothesis: Increasing perceived social support leads to higher quality of life among parents of children with ASD, and this effect is partially mediated by increased psychological resilience. Related Work: Existing research consistently reports positive associations between social support, resilience, and parental quality of life in caregivers of children with developmental disabilities. Typical methods include cross-sectional correlation/regression analyses, single-site surveys, and occasional structural equation models testing mediation. Prior approaches commonly rely on self-report scales (e.g., SSRS, CD-RISC, WHOQOL-BREF) and bootstrap tests for indirect effects. Limitations in the literature include frequent use of single-region or convenience samples, predominance of cross-sectional designs that preclude temporal/causal inference, limited tests of measurement invariance or alternative mediator/moderator models, insufficient comparison of analytic methods (PROCESS macro versus latent-variable SEM or cross-lagged models), and narrow operationalizations of resilience (often individual-level only). Few studies evaluate robustness to confounders (child ASD severity, parent demographics) or examine generalizability across cultural and service-access contexts. Abstract: This study addresses whether resilience mediates the relationship between perceived social support and quality of life (QoL) in parents of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in China. We propose a quantitative mediation framework that models social support as the independent variable, resilience as the mediator, and multidomain QoL as the outcome. The primary contribution is an explicit, testable pipeline for evaluating direct and indirect effects using both regression-based bootstrapped mediation and latent-variable structural equation modeling, including specification checks and alternative mediator comparisons. Expected outputs include standardized direct and indirect effect estimates, confidence intervals for mediation, model fit indices, and sensitivity analyses across instrument variants and sample stratifications. The anticipated impact is improved empirical clarity about the pathway linking external supports to parental well-being and a validated analytic protocol for subsequent longitudinal and intervention research. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Original cross-sectional dataset: N=257 parents recruited from a hospital-based outpatient rehabilitation registry (measures: SSRS total and subscales, CD-RISC total, WHOQOL-BREF domains, demographics, child ASD severity). (B) Replication cross-sectional multi-site dataset: target N>=500 across at least 3 regions. (C) Longitudinal panel: 3 waves (baseline, 6 months, 12 months) target N>=350 with retention >70%. Include a matched control group of parents of typically developing children (matched on parent age, gender, education). Baselines: (1) Direct-effect model (social support -> QoL), (2) Mediation via resilience (PROCESS Model 4), (3) Latent-variable SEM mediation, (4) Alternative mediator models (e.g., parental self-efficacy, caregiving burden), (5) Moderation models (resilience as moderator), (6) Cross-lagged panel model for directionality. Evaluation metrics: standardized regression coefficients (β), indirect effect size and proportion mediated, bootstrap 95% CI for indirect effect (5000 resamples), R2 and change in R2, SEM fit indices (CFI ≥0.95, TLI ≥0.95, RMSEA ≤0.06, SRMR ≤0.08), AIC/BIC for model comparison, Cohen's f2 for effect size, measurement invariance indices across subgroups. Experimental setup: data cleaning and descriptive checks; handle missing data with multiple imputation (m=20) and compare with full-information ML for SEM; standardize primary variables; include covariates (parent gender, age, education, employment status, child age, ASD severity) in all models; run PROCESS Model 4 with 5000 bootstrap samples; fit latent-variable SEM in lavaan (or equivalent) with resilience and social support as latent constructs when subscale items available; perform ablation studies: (i) remove support subscales one at a time (objective, subjective, utilization), (ii) replace CD-RISC with an alternative resilience measure, (iii) compare mediation magnitude between hospital-only and multi-site samples, (iv) test cross-lagged directional paths in longitudinal panel. Report subgroup analyses (mother vs father, ASD severity strata) and sensitivity to unmeasured confounding using bias-correction methods (e.g., E-value). Risk Factors and Limitations: Cross-sectional causal inference limitations: temporal ordering cannot be established from cross-sectional data; risk of reverse causation. Self-report measurement bias: common-method variance, social desirability, and differential interpretation of items across cultural subgroups. Sample bias and generalizability: single-site hospital samples may not represent rural or under-resourced populations; multi-site recruitment increases complexity and heterogeneity. Measurement invariance: resilience and QoL instruments may not be measurement-invariant across subgroups, limiting valid comparisons. Omitted variable/confounding risk: unmeasured factors (e.g., parental mental health history, family functioning, service access) may bias mediation estimates. Statistical/modeling risks: model misspecification, nonlinearity, multicollinearity among predictors, and small subgroup cell sizes reduce power. Longitudinal attrition: differential dropout may induce bias in panel estimates. Computational limits: latent-variable SEM with many items and bootstrapping is computationally intensive. Ethical constraints: sensitive participant data and stigma risks require robust confidentiality and informed consent procedures.
